description:
23 July 2015: Observed a single Yellow-billed Cuckoo (Coccyzus americanus) perched up a tree branch at Elm Fork Park, Greenbelt Corridor, Lake Ray Roberts/Lake Lewisville State Park, Access Area FM 455, Denton County, Texas (between Pilot Point and Sanger, Texas).

This was my first observation in the wild of this bird and the first time I've observed the Yellow-billed Cuckoo at Elm Fork Park. The bird was perched a distance away which explains the digital image. And it only gave me opportunity to take but two digital frames before flying off thus living up to its reported secretive nature. Among the insects they prefer to eat are cicadas and there were plenty of cicadas at Elm Fork Park loudly announcing their presence. Hundreds of dragonflies were flying as well in the area where this bird was sighted. 

Mark Lockwood of the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department prepared a "Birds of Ray Roberts Lake State Park: A Field Checklist" (January 2010) that's available online here: https://tpwd.texas.gov/publications/pwdpubs/media/pwd_bk_p4503_0137u.pdf . Lockwood determined that the Yellow-billed Cuckoo is "common" at this site during spring, summer and fall.

The Yellow-billed Cuckoo is a true migrant and bird of the Americas, an American bird writ large, since it occurs from the most southeastern corner of Canada's provinces and on into or across the eastern half of the United States (with reduced presence in specific sites of various states in the US West). The bird's extensive wintering migration ranges widely continuing into Mexico through Texas primarily (where this bird is presumably found throughout the entire state) and Central and South America as far as the northern reaches of Argentina. The only country in South America where the Yellow-billed Cuckoo reportedly does not fly is Chile. The Caribbean island nations are also home for the Yellow-billed Cuckoo. This bird is native to most countries in the Western Hemisphere. In Texas, it is generally present from April to October, though it is considered to be far less common west of Central Texas.

In the United States its presence in the West and to a lesser but notable extent in the East has been declining for decades. During the first half of the 20th century the Yellow-billed Cuckoo disappeared entirely from the Pacific Northwest of the United States and Canada's far Southwest (British Columbia, Washington, and Oregon).

Elm Fork Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (TPWD).

Sources: All About Birds - Cornell Lab of Ornithology, BirdLife International, Texas Breeding Bird Atlas, and Wikipedia.

Another day of a Yellow-billed Cuckoo escort on my hiking trails. They are one of the most acrobatic flyers on the late summer ridge.

I had a surprise encounter appear in a blackberry thicket right next to my trail. A fledgling Yellow-billed Cuckoo had assumed a frozen posture hoping I wouldn't notice it trying to blend into the background. As I moved around it to get a better view through the leaves, it never moved a muscle or even blinked as I got my photo. I moved away a few feet to see if it would relax, but it never did as long as I was in sight. A whole new experience for me on another day on the ridge.
This just hit our window. I’m not sure what it is.

A Yellow-billed Cuckoo joins me on the wagon road path. They tend to go about their business as I pass by and show little fear or curiosity in me. I have no doubt that they consider me nothing more than some mutant deer.

description: The *kook-kook-kook* call repeated in the recording, amidst the din of cicadas.

I've been watching Yellow-billed Cuckoos for a long time, but this was the first I had seen on the ground. 

I am very curious about the plumage and soft parts of this bird: the bill has as much yellow as any adult, but I can see no sign of yellow in the orbital ring. And there are some plumage oddities: slight indication of short streaking in the throat area, a tuft at the top of its head, various smudges on the underparts and the look of somewhat sparse feathering on the belly and legs. So is it a bird of the year, or an adult starting (or about to start) prebasic molt? Opinions welcome, please.

description:
Fledgling wet and bedraggled making frog noises out front. Warmed and dried. Took some banana and two live larvae.

Last three shots are release shots. After ten days of hourly feedings and the last two days in an oak sapling in my laundry room the cuckoo is free. Rapid growth. She learned to take mealworms, grubs and sawfly cats off leaf surfaces quickly. And in the tree she did the slow cuckoo scan of the leaves. 

Fly well cuckoo. One of my favorite birds.

description:
A solo visit -- Deer Run Road is no longer flooded over, so it was an easy drive in. The weather at the start was sunny and 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), with a light breeze/occasionally breezy. I walked the northern leg of the nature trail (flooded in places), then walked north along the powerlines, then northeast-curving-southeast to the eastern entrance, then west along the fenceline. After I crossed the powerlines, in an area that burned in spring 2024, I was astounded by the number of Coastal Plain Honeycombead plants. I easily searched 2,000 individual flowers for Fuller's Flower Moths, finding ZERO! But, I found two Alluring Flower Moths, photographing one with my camera.

These are my camera photographs (49 of them), which will be given a generic time (1200, when I started) and a generic location (a circle that does not include any non-WEA area). I took more than 500 cell-phone photographs, which will take several days for me to cull and post. I left at 1549 and headed home.

Note: due to the abundance of Purple Passionflower onsite, there are large number of Gulf Fritllaries; each record here is believed to represent a different individual.

Along the fenceline east of the parking area, where a yappy little dog annoyed me.

With Valeri Ponzo; a day-trip to boost our Gilchrist County lists (40 for Val and 37 for me) to over 49 species. The park opens at 0900 so we left Spring Hill to arrive ~10 minutes before the park opened. But while waiting for the gate to be opened, I checked the park website and discovered that the park is closed because most of the trails are flooded. We drove to the RV Campground and tried to access that area, but the campground was just mowed grass; the trails between the park and campground were also flooded. So we birded the RV entrance road, finding a number of birds -- but they were very active and flighty; I got very few photographs. We can only wonder what we missed by the park being closed. We will be back some other fall day ... The weather was clear and mild with a light breeze. We left at 1005 after 1 hour and 15 minutes, and headed to Gilchrist Blue Springs State Park.
